content: The World Health Organization (WHO) developed updated guidelines in July 2018 for the care and treatment of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. As part of the evidence-gathering process, WHO conducted online surveys targeting three groups: individuals living with HCV, healthcare workers (HCWs) providing care to HCV patients, and national program managers. These surveys aimed to assess the acceptability, feasibility, and preferences related to the recommendations in the guidelines. The findings from these surveys contributed to the evidence base for the recommendations. Survey Design and Implementation Three online surveys were created using the SurveyMonkey® platform and were available in English and French. The surveys were piloted internally, and adjustments were made before dissemination. The target groups for the surveys were as follows: 1. People living with HCV infection: Key civil society networks and guideline development group members were contacted, and snowball sampling was encouraged. 2. Healthcare workers (HCWs): Networks providing care to HCV patients and guideline development group members were approached to disseminate the survey. 3. Program managers: Surveys were sent to national program managers through WHO regional offices and advisors. Survey Results Survey 1: People Living with HCV Infection A total of 112 individuals responded, with 70% being male and over 80% aged between 30 and 60 years. Respondents represented all WHO regions except the Eastern Mediterranean, with fewer participants from the African and European regions. Among respondents, 87% reported receiving antiviral treatment for HCV, while 13% were aware of their infection but had not yet been treated. Of those treated, 65% received care in hospital settings, and 25% in private clinics. When asked about a potential treat all policy (where all HCV-diagnosed patients would receive antiviral treatment regardless of disease stage), 20% indicated their clinic already had such a policy, and 30% expressed no concerns. However, some respondents raised concerns about drug-drug interactions (20%), long-term side effects (17%), treatment acceptability (17%), and costs (16%). Survey 2: Healthcare Workers A total of 145 HCWs from 27 countries responded, representing all WHO regions. Respondents included hospital physicians (40%), primary care physicians (25%), private clinic physicians (15%), nurses (11%), and other roles. Half of the HCWs reported that their workplace already implemented a treat all policy. The most commonly perceived challenges were capacity limitations to meet demand (30%), difficulties identifying eligible patients, lack of HCW skills, and issues with patient adherence and retention in care. Survey 3: Program Managers Ten program managers from countries including Brazil, Cameroon, Colombia, Egypt, Georgia, Iceland, Morocco, Pakistan, South Africa, and Zimbabwe responded. All reported having viral hepatitis strategies and action plans in place, with three countries treating people in prisons and one country offering specialized clinics for people who inject drugs. Half of the program managers indicated that their country already had a treat all policy. The main challenges identified were a lack of testing strategies, insufficient funding, lack of HCW skills, and difficulties identifying eligible patients. Key Findings A treat all policy was widely perceived as feasible and desirable by individuals living with HCV, HCWs, and program managers. Among individuals living with HCV, the most common concerns were potential drug-drug interactions, long-term side effects, treatment acceptability, and costs. For HCWs, the greatest challenges were capacity limitations, identifying eligible patients, and costs. Program managers highlighted the lack of testing strategies and funding as the most significant barriers to implementing a treat all policy.
